This asymptotic size contrasts with the length at which reproductive development begins, as gonadal maturation is initiated at a total length of 67.5 centimeters [Lp = 67.5 centimeters], indicating a substantial period of somatic growth prior to the onset of sexual maturity. The difference between these two length measurements suggests that individuals allocate considerable resources to attaining body size before shifting investment toward gamete production, a life-history strategy common among pelagic predators operating in food-limited environments. Field surveys of the central Pacific have recorded specimens spanning this entire size range, confirming that the species follows a determinate growth trajectory typical of iteroparous teleosts.

Gravid females produce pelagic eggs that hatch into yolk-sac larvae weighing just 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams] at the moment of eclosion, an exceptionally low neonatal mass that reflects the tiny egg diameter characteristic of this lineage. The ultimate wet weight of adult Sickle pomfret reaches 17,000 grams [Wwi = 17,000 grams], corresponding to the maximum female length of 92 centimeters through a length-weight conversion that aligns with general bramid allometry. This considerable body mass supports the energetic demands of protracted migrations and deep-water foraging, as adults are frequently captured at depths exceeding 200 meters where they prey upon cephalopods and mesopelagic fishes. Available data suggest that females continue to add mass incrementally even after attaining sexual maturity, though growth rate slows considerably beyond the pubertal length of 67.5 centimeters. Comparative records from the temperate Pacific indicate that this asymptotic mass is among the highest recorded within the genus Taractichthys, possibly reflecting the relatively stable prey base available in subtropical gyre systems.

At a sustained water temperature of 15.2 °C [T = 15.2 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan for Sickle pomfret is 8 years [am = 8 years], a longevity that aligns with the moderate pace of life expected for a large-bodied, late-maturing pelagic fish. This value was documented through otolith annuli analysis of specimens collected across the species' range in the North Pacific, where slow annual growth increments in older individuals confirmed the attainment of this age. The combination of a relatively extended lifespan, a late pubertal length of 67.5 centimeters [Lp = 67.5 centimeters], and the high daily fecundity of 1,397 eggs per day [Ri = 1,397 eggs per day] under those same thermal conditions reveals a life-history strategy that prioritizes both longevity and reproductive output, a pattern that is comparatively rare among epipelagic fishes.
